column3: Directly pairs mercy with enjoyment until a specified time, matching the focus's bounded preservation.
Contrasts believers' merciful benefit with wrongdoers' loss, clarifying the divergent reception behind the focus's belief.
Shares earthly enjoyment until a time, though here it follows descent and enmity rather than collective belief.
Defines enjoyment until a time as a possible test, supplying the focus's alternative temporal valence.
Begins the immediate Yunus sequence whose restored mission culminates in 37:148.
Links turning back to God with good enjoyment until an appointed term.
Explicitly identifies Yunus's people: they believed, punishment was removed, and they enjoyed life until a time.
The immediately preceding dispatch names the large people who believe in the focus ayah.
Contrasts others' temporary enjoyments with care for believers, framing enjoyment as no basis for envy.
A people are told to enjoy themselves only until a time, a warning-side counterpart to the focus's mercy.
Yunus's flight to the laden ship is an immediate earlier stage in the narrative resolved at 37:148.
Shows a divided response of belief and rejection, whereas the focus reports a people who collectively believed.
Commands belief in God, the messenger, and the revealed light, supplying the response named in the focus.
Rescue of Lot's household amid judgment parallels preservation as the alternative to a community's destruction.
Its rebuke for scant belief supplies only a general negative counterpart to the focus's belief.
Presents belief in the messenger who brings truth as good for its recipients.
The lot that Yunus loses is an immediate narrative step before his recovery and restored dispatch.
Fear of punishment does not materially clarify belief, enjoyment, or the limited term in the focus.

The cloud-formation branch resonance adds no focused account of Yunus's community, belief, or enjoyment.
The rejected safety-to-belief reading is not positive evidence for the focus.
Calls all people to believe in God and His messenger and follow him for guidance.
Yunus being swallowed while blameworthy is an immediate earlier stage of the sequence completed by the focus.
It shares an unspecified period of waiting but concerns Joseph's imprisonment, not preserved enjoyment.
Calls for corrected belief in God and His messengers, furnishing a doctrinal counterpart to the focus's response.
The temporal observation scene and its branch resonance do not clarify the focus's communal outcome.
The same surah's command to withdraw until a time supplies the rejecting side of the focus's twofold limited interval.
Its repeated withdrawal-until-a-time command frames a deferred outcome for those who do not respond.
Yunus's prior praise explains why his ordeal did not continue until resurrection.
Its question about what message people will believe sharpens the significance of the focus's affirmative response.
Leaving deniers in heedlessness until a time gives the adverse counterpart to the focus's preserved believers.
Gathering and hoarding do not add a usable route to the focus's belief or time-bounded enjoyment.
Patience and praise at a time offer only a remote temporal parallel to the focus.
Years of enjoyment do not avert the eventual promised consequence, clarifying the limit on temporal benefit.
States the counterfactual duration of Yunus's confinement, directly framing his later restoration.
A distress-driven claim of belief is a limited contrast to the focus's effective communal belief.
The promised news becomes known after a time, reinforcing that delayed outcomes are temporally appointed.
Disbelief increases loss over time, contrasting with the focus's belief and continued enjoyment.
Links belief and righteous action to freedom from fear and grief, an outcome-side parallel to preservation.
Divine respite shows that delay is not acquittal, clarifying the focus's bounded term.
Yunus's sick casting onto the open shore is an immediate recovery stage before his renewed mission.
It depicts believers under persecution, offering only a general contrast to the focus's protected community.
Temporary enjoyment is followed by compelled severe punishment, the judgment-side contrast to the focus.
A community's refusal after a warner arrives contrasts with the focus's successful response to dispatch.
Being seen while standing provides only an incidental time expression, not the focus's outcome pattern.
Brief enjoyment followed by painful punishment defines a negative form of the focus's limited enjoyment.
The gourd grown over Yunus is immediate restorative care before he is sent again.
Creation as a sign for believers gives only general evidentiary context for belief.
Earthly settlement and enjoyment until a time parallel the focus's finite worldly duration in a different setting.
The Quraysh travel-alliance reference does not clarify belief, preservation, or the stated term.
Worldly enjoyment is explicitly little before its final consequence, defining its limited value.
The marital provision rule does not contribute to the focus's communal belief-and-preservation pattern.
The crushing of mountains has no focused link to belief, enjoyment, or Yunus's restored mission.
A messenger calls his community to worship, justice, and faith, paralleling the mission whose recipients believe in the focus.
Earthly goods are temporary enjoyment, while lasting good is for believers who rely on their Lord.
The division into three groups does not materially clarify the focus's limited enjoyment.
People who reject after rescue are left to enjoy themselves and later know, a direct negative counterpart.
Useful dwellings and goods are explicitly enjoyment until a time, extending the finite-use motif.
The ransom fantasy does not clarify the focus's belief, mercy, or specified interval.
Questions raised during revelation do not add to the focus's belief-and-enjoyment relation.
Deniers defer judgment on a messenger until a time, contrasting with the focus's community accepting its messenger.
The call for beautiful patience has no specific route to the focus's communal outcome.
Provision's expansion and restriction are signs for believers, but not a focused account of bounded enjoyment.
The livestock routine uses time incidentally and adds no relevant relation.
The angels' ascent over a vast day does not clarify the focus's finite earthly term.
Belief compromised by association contrasts with the effective belief reported for Yunus's people.
The rhetorical challenge to disbelief highlights the affirmative communal belief in the focus.
The trusted messenger description does not clarify the focus's response or outcome.
Regular praise at evening and morning is only an incidental temporal parallel.
God responds to believers who do good and increases them from His favor, an outcome-side belief parallel.
It calls worldly enjoyment little compared with the Hereafter, directly qualifying the value of the focus's term.
The human's unmentioned time before existence does not clarify the focus's temporal mercy.
Moses's entry at an unguarded time has no material relation to the focus.
Enjoyment amid ingratitude is permitted only until later knowledge, a warning-side counterpart.
Even disbelievers receive brief worldly enjoyment before punishment, contrasting material respite with final standing.
A sign is identified for believers, supplying general evidence-response context for the focus's belief.
Deniers' eventual confrontation with fire gives only a broad deferred-outcome contrast.
Belief joined to righteous action yields the highest ranks, showing belief's enduring positive consequence.
Belief here means trust in a disputed report and does not clarify the focus's religious response.
Joseph rejects a people who disbelieve in God and the Hereafter, a general contrast to the focus's believers.
Believers enter gardens while disbelievers merely enjoy and consume before the Fire, directly contrasting outcomes.
Fruit produced at every time offers a temporal motif but no focused relation to communal belief or respite.
Lives are released until an appointed term, providing a direct frame for finite extension of life.
Noah is named among believing servants in the same surah's rescue pattern, a parallel prophetic preservation account.
The testament procedure's time reference does not contribute to the focus.
Belief made visible in righteous action receives a superior enduring evaluation.
Concealment from divine knowledge has no focused relation to the belief and enjoyment sequence.
Abraham's identity as a believing servant offers a same-surah prophetic faith parallel.
Household etiquette and material requests do not clarify the focus's bounded enjoyment.

Hearers recognize recitation as truth and declare belief, closely paralleling a community's affirmative reception.
Some turn away when summoned to God and His messenger for judgment, contrasting with the focus's response.
Entrenched refusal to believe contrasts sharply with the exceptional belief of Yunus's people in the adjacent passage.
Return to God for final judgment supplies the endpoint beyond the focus's temporary enjoyment.
Worldly adornment is temporary enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Excessive love of wealth loosely contrasts with treating finite goods as temporary rather than ultimate.
Disbelief in the Hereafter is paired with prepared painful punishment, the negative final outcome beyond temporal respite.
The resurrection emergence scene does not materially clarify the focus's belief or limited enjoyment.
Faithful striving for the Hereafter is acknowledged, giving belief an enduring reward beyond temporary enjoyment.
Abundance granted until a people rejoice is followed by sudden seizure, defining enjoyment as neither approval nor security.
Mutual use continues until an appointed term, extending the focus's finite-duration frame to a corrupt alliance.
Worldly enjoyment is explicitly temporary before return to God and the consequence of disbelief.
Nations receive temporal enjoyment after Noah's rescue, yet some later receive painful punishment; this closely parallels the focus's preserved community.
Thamud are allowed enjoyment for three days before the promised consequence, a precise warning-side temporal counterpart.
Those who set up rivals are told to enjoy themselves before the Fire, directly contrasting temporary use with final outcome.
One who seeks the immediate world may receive it briefly before Hell, qualifying worldly grant as a final good.
Worldly splendor is not to be coveted; the Lord's provision is better and more enduring than temporary enjoyment.
Yunus's departure, distress, and prayer supply the other principal Quranic account behind his restored mission in the focus.
God answers and saves Yunus from distress, then generalizes this saving pattern to believers.
The present life is stated to be temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is the lasting abode.
Worldly life is described as passing play, adornment, rivalry, and deceptive enjoyment, directly qualifying the focus's term.
It explicitly recalls Yunus as the companion of the fish, supplying the third principal account of his ordeal.
Divine grace prevents Yunus from being cast onto open ground in a blameworthy state, paralleling his restoration.
Yunus is chosen and made righteous after his ordeal, completing the recovery that precedes the focus's successful dispatch.
